2026-04-20_25-466_sripetch-v-sec_decisio.title: 6/4/26 – Decision: Sripetch v. Securities and Exchange Commission (9 to 0)
2026-04-20_25-466_sripetch-v-sec_decisio.description: - Decided: June 4, 2026 - Vote: 9 to 0 - Majority: Gorsuch, for a unanimous Court - Concurrences: Thomas, alone. Argues that once Congress added section 78u d 7 in 2021 and separated "disgorgement" from "equitable remedies" in the limitations provisions, disgorgement became a legal remedy for which the Seventh Amendment requires a jury trial; urges the Court to so hold in a future case and describes the SEC's practice of sending disgorged funds to the Treasury as a fines regime. - Dissents: None.

2026-10-05_25-170_suncor-v-boulder.title: 10/5/26 – Prep: Suncor Energy (U.S.A.) Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County
2026-10-05_25-170_suncor-v-boulder.description: Boulder County and the City of Boulder sued Suncor and ExxonMobil in Colorado state court in 2018, pleading public and private nuisance, trespass, unjust enrichment, civil conspiracy, and Colorado Consumer Protection Act claims, and seeking damages for local climate-adaptation costs, heat, drought, wildfire, reduced snowpack, they attribute to the companies' production and marketing of fossil fuels. After a removal fight that ended with the case back in state court, the trial court denied the companies' motion to dismiss on preemption grounds. In May 2025 the Colorado Supreme Court held that neither federal common law, the Clean Air Act, nor the federal foreign-affairs power bars the claims, reasoning that Boulder seeks compensation for the companies' conduct rather than regulation of anyone's emissions. The Court granted certiorari on February 23, 2026 and directed the parties to also address whether the interlocutory ruling is a reviewable final judgment under section 1257 and whether petitioners have Article Three standing. Roughly two dozen similar suits by states and municipalities are pending nationwide; the Trump administration filed an amicus brief supporting the companies, and more than 100 amicus briefs were filed in all.
2026-10-05_25-170_suncor-v-boulder.art_label: Suncor Energy v. Boulder County · Oct 5

2026-10-05_25-735_johnson-v-us-congress.title: 10/5/26 – Prep: Johnson v. United States Congress
2026-10-05_25-735_johnson-v-us-congress.description: Johnson received an 80 percent VA disability rating for service-connected PTSD. After he was convicted of state felonies and sentenced to 40 years, the VA reduced his compensation to the 10 percent rate under section 5313, which caps benefits for veterans incarcerated more than 60 days for a felony. Proceeding pro se, he sued Congress in the Middle District of Florida, alleging that section 5313 is a bill of attainder and denies equal protection; a magistrate judge recommended dismissal as frivolous and the district court agreed. The Eleventh Circuit vacated and ordered dismissal for want of jurisdiction, holding that section 511 a of the VJRA channels all claims touching veterans' benefits, including facial constitutional challenges to statutes, through the VA, the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims, and the Federal Circuit. That ruling aligned the Eleventh Circuit with the Eighth and against the Second, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Ninth, and D.C. Circuits, which read Robison as preserving district-court jurisdiction over constitutional challenges to the statutes themselves. The government agreed that certiorari was warranted while defending the Eleventh Circuit on the merits; the Court granted on April 6, 2026. Eight amicus briefs support Johnson; none supports the government.

2026-10-06_25-498_anderson-v-intel.title: 10/6/26 – Prep: Anderson v. Intel Corp. Investment Policy Committee
2026-10-06_25-498_anderson-v-intel.description: After the 2008 financial crisis, Intel's investment committee redesigned the plans' custom target-date funds and a diversified fund to allocate substantial shares, plaintiffs say roughly a third of some funds, to hedge funds, private equity, commodities, and other alternative assets, with the stated goal of dampening equity volatility. Participants sued in 2019, alleging the funds carried higher fees and chronically underperformed conventional target-date funds, peer-group averages, and market indices with heavier equity exposure, and that the fiduciaries breached ERISA's duties of prudence and loyalty. The district court dismissed for failure to plead a "meaningful benchmark," and the Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that an underperformance claim must identify a comparator with similar aims, risks, and potential rewards, and that broad indices and ordinary target-date funds were not meaningful benchmarks for funds built to reduce equity risk. The Second, Seventh, Eighth, and Tenth Circuits apply versions of the same requirement; the Sixth Circuit declined to make a benchmark a pleading prerequisite in Johnson versus Parker-Hannifin Corporation, from 2024, and a cert petition in that case is pending. The Court granted certiorari on January 16, 2026, and the United States filed as amicus supporting Intel.

2026-10-07_25-579_air-force-v-prutehi-gu.title: 10/7/26 – Prep: Department of the Air Force v. Prutehi Guåhan
2026-10-07_25-579_air-force-v-prutehi-gu.description: Since the 1980s the Air Force has disposed of expired and unexploded munitions by open burning and open detonation at Tarague Beach on Andersen Air Force Base in northern Guam, under a RCRA hazardous-waste permit administered by Guam EPA, which holds EPA-authorized permitting authority. In May 2021 the Air Force applied to renew the permit; Guam EPA issued a preliminary decision that October that neither granted nor denied it, and the application remains pending while operations continue under the expired permit. Prutehi Guåhan sued in January 2022, alleging the Air Force violated NEPA by failing to prepare an environmental impact statement before applying. The District of Guam dismissed for lack of final agency action, but a divided Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the application marked the consummation of the Air Force's decision to continue detonations and carried legal consequences under Bennett versus Spear, and that RCRA's permitting process does not displace NEPA; Judge VanDyke dissented that the application was a routine step in implementing an existing operation and that the majority's approach could reach almost any agency decision. The Court granted certiorari on March 9, 2026. Amici for the government include the Chamber of Commerce and 21 states led by West Virginia; amici for respondent include 11 states led by Washington, Guam and Pacific-territory community organizations, members of Congress, and the Virgin Islands Bar Association.
2026-10-07_25-579_air-force-v-prutehi-gu.art_label: Air Force v. Prutehi Guåhan · Oct 7

2026-10-13_25-5343_beaird-v-us.title: 10/13/26 – Prep: Beaird v. United States
2026-10-13_25-5343_beaird-v-us.description: In October 2022, Dallas police took a Glock pistol with an inserted 17-round magazine from Kendrick Beaird's waistband, the government says an officer saw him point it at another person; Beaird stresses that the gun was unloaded and the magazine was the factory standard, and he pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm as a felon under section 922 g 1. Guideline section 2K2.1 a 3 raises the base offense level when the offense involved a semiautomatic firearm "capable of accepting a large capacity magazine," a phrase the guideline text does not define but Application Note 2 of the commentary defines as a magazine that could accept more than 15 rounds; applying the note raised Beaird's range from 51 to 63 to 63 to 78 months, and the district court imposed 72 months while stating it would have imposed the same sentence under any range. The Fifth Circuit summarily affirmed, treating the challenge as foreclosed by United States versus Vargas, en banc 2023, which held that Stinson survives Kisor versus Wilkie and that commentary controls even unambiguous guidelines, and by United States versus Martin, from 2024, which upheld this particular note. The circuits have divided over whether Kisor's limits apply to Guidelines commentary, though the government notes that every circuit to apply Kisor to the large-capacity-magazine note has upheld it. Neither party defends the judgment, Beaird argues for no deference at all, or, alternatively, Kisor's limits, and the United States argues that Stinson properly incorporates Kisor's limits and supports vacatur and remand while predicting the same sentence, so the Court appointed Anthony Dick to argue that Stinson remains correct as written.

2026-10-14_25-459_salazar-v-paramount.title: 10/14/26 – Prep: Salazar v. Paramount Global
2026-10-14_25-459_salazar-v-paramount.description: In 2022 Michael Salazar signed up for a free email newsletter from 247Sports.com, a Paramount-owned college-sports site; he alleges that when he later watched videos on the site while logged into Facebook, the Meta Pixel embedded in the site sent Facebook his Facebook ID and the addresses of the video pages he viewed without his consent, and he seeks the VPPA's $2,500 in liquidated damages per class member plus punitive damages. The district court dismissed on the ground that he was not a "consumer" because the newsletter was not audiovisual, and a divided Sixth Circuit affirmed: Judge Nalbandian, joined by Judge Batchelder, read "goods or services from a video tape service provider" together with the statute's definition of a provider as one dealing in "prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials" and held that only audiovisual goods or services count, while Judge Bloomekatz dissented that the plain text limits the source of the goods or services, not their type. The circuits are split 2 to 2: the Second Circuit, in Salazar versus NBA, a parallel suit by the same plaintiff, and the Seventh Circuit read the definition to reach any of a provider's goods or services, including newsletters, while the D.C. Circuit sided with the Sixth in Pileggi versus Washington Newspaper Publishing Company, where a cert petition is pending. In opposing certiorari, Paramount argued the claim would fail anyway because 247Sports is not a "video tape service provider" and Pixel data is not "personally identifiable information," but the courts below assumed both points, the Sixth Circuit decided only the "consumer" question, and Paramount's merits brief does not press the alternative grounds. The Court denied the NBA's petition raising the same "consumer" question, along with a standing question, on December 8, 2025, and granted this one on January 26, 2026.

2026-11-02_25-352_younge-v-fulton-da.title: 11/2/26 – Prep: Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office, Georgia
2026-11-02_25-352_younge-v-fulton-da.description: In April 2019 Fulton County District Attorney Paul Howard hired Jasmine Younge as his Deputy Chief of Staff and Director of Policy and Programs, the third-ranking job in the office. She supervised more than thirty employees, reported only to Howard and testified that she was his "go-to person for almost everything." On about July 1 she told Howard she was pregnant. She alleges that he reacted angrily, cut her out of meetings and reassigned her duties, and he fired her on July 15. Howard testified that he had already told her she was not working out; his chief of staff testified she knew of no discussion of firing Younge before the announcement. The office answered Younge's Title Seven suit, N.D. Ga.; her other claims were dismissed or abandoned, on March 24, 2021. The answer listed several affirmative defenses but not the section 2000e f personal-staff exemption, although it admitted she was a member of the DA's "executive and/or personal staff." The scheduling order's deadline to amend pleadings passed on May 26, 2021, and discovery closed January 5, 2022. At a March 14, 2022 discovery hearing the office first said it would rely on the exemption; counsel said he had not realized it was an issue until he began drafting the summary judgment motion. On May 16, 2022 it moved for summary judgment on that exemption and on the separate "policymaking appointee" exemption, without ever seeking leave to amend. Applying Hassan versus U.S. Postal Service, the magistrate judge treated the exemption as an affirmative defense and found it had not been pleaded or noticed before March 2022. She still found no prejudice, because the extra discovery Younge proposed concerned facts within her own knowledge, was a "fishing expedition," or amounted to legal research. She declined to reach the policymaking-appointee exemption, finding that late assertion prejudicial, and recommended summary judgment on the personal-staff ground. The district court agreed, granting summary judgment even though it found sufficient evidence of discriminatory motive. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed. It assumed without deciding that the exemption is an affirmative defense, noting that the Fourth and Fifth Circuits disagree on that point, and reaffirmed Hassan's rule that a court may consider an unpleaded affirmative defense at summary judgment if the plaintiff is not prejudiced. It found no prejudice, stressing that Younge never took up the magistrate judge's offer to reopen discovery and had conceded that the office's discovery responses referred to her as "personal staff" five times. In footnote 8 it rejected her argument that Rule 16 b 4's good-cause standard applied: "we simply treat unpleaded affirmative defenses differently from late motions to amend pleadings." On the merits, assuming the six-factor Laurie test governs, it held that there was no genuine dispute that she was Howard's personal staff.

2026-11-02_25-5930_maxwell-v-dinis.title: 11/2/26 – Prep: Maxwell v. Dinis
2026-11-02_25-5930_maxwell-v-dinis.description: Maxwell, a former lawyer, was convicted by a New Jersey federal jury in 2014 of RICO conspiracy, wire fraud and related counts arising from a scheme with members of La Cosa Nostra to take control of FirstPlus Financial Group, a Texas mortgage lender, and drain more than $14 million from it; he was sentenced in 2015 to 240 months plus three years of supervised release, the Third Circuit affirmed, United States versus Scarfo, from 2022, and he disputes the government's account of the conduct in a pending section 2255 motion. He has no disciplinary infractions, carries B O P's lowest recidivism-risk rating, and has worked as a cook and a law-library clerk, activities he says earn First Step Act time credits, which the Act says "shall be applied toward time in prerelease custody or supervised release", section 3632 d 4 C. After B O P denied his requests, beginning in 2020, for transfer to a halfway house or home confinement, he filed a pro se section 2241 petition in February 2022 alleging, among other things, that B O P was not counting some of his productive activities and owed him 42 to 48 months of credits. The magistrate judge and district court dismissed: the First Step Act claims were unexhausted because his grievances sought only CARES Act home confinement, and the CARES Act claim failed on the merits. The government defended the dismissal on exhaustion alone, but the Fifth Circuit affirmed on a ground neither side had raised: under the "bright-line rule" of Melot versus Bergami, a claim belongs in habeas only if success would automatically entitle the prisoner to accelerated release, so a request for a halfway house or home confinement must be brought as a civil-rights, Bivens, suit. It did not reach exhaustion, and in a footnote it set aside an unpublished contrary ruling on CARES Act home confinement, Cheek versus Warden, and described Maxwell's claim as arising under the First Step Act's elderly-offender pilot program, a description Maxwell disputed.

2026-11-03_25-581_st-mary-v-roy.title: 11/3/26 – Prep: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy
2026-11-03_25-581_st-mary-v-roy.description: After Colorado voters approved Proposition EE in 2020, the legislature created a Department of Early Childhood and a universal preschool program that pays for 15 hours a week of preschool for every four-year-old at any participating provider, public, private, or faith-based, in a "mixed delivery" system of nearly 2,000 preschools. Every provider must meet statutory quality standards, including that it "provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability," Colorado Revised Statutes section 26.5-4-205 2 b. Families rank up to five preschools and an algorithm matches them; by regulation the Department lets providers apply enrollment "preferences", for congregation members, since repealed; cooperative families; district boundaries; children with IEPs; Head Start-eligible low-income families; employees' children, continuing students and siblings; multilingual children; and a catchall for other Department-approved criteria, so long as they comply with the equal-opportunity requirement, and more than 1,000 providers use at least one. More than forty faith-based providers, including six Archdiocese-affiliated Catholic Charities preschools, joined in the first year. The Archdiocese's parish preschools require families to sign a statement committing to support Catholic teaching, including on sexuality, marriage, and gender; petitioners' witnesses testified that the schools would not enroll children of same-sex parents and would not continue enrolling a child who came to identify with a gender different from the child's biological sex. In early 2023 the Archdiocese told its preschools not to register, a coalition of faith-based providers asked for a religious exemption, and Executive Director Roy replied that she lacked authority to create one.

2026-11-04_25-1003_guerrero-v-johnson.title: 11/4/26 – Prep: Guerrero v. Johnson
2026-11-04_25-1003_guerrero-v-johnson.description: In June 2006, in Houston, Dexter Johnson and four companions abducted 23-year-old Maria Aparece and her boyfriend, Huy Ngo, at gunpoint. Johnson raped Aparece, and both victims were shot in the head in a wooded area. Johnson was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death in 2007, five years after Atkins versus Virginia barred executing people with intellectual disability. At the punishment phase his own expert, Dr. Dale Watson, put his IQ between 74 and 88 and testified that he was not intellectually disabled under the then-governing DSM-IV-TR framework. Texas stresses that Watson saw no obvious adaptive deficits; Johnson says the IQ scores ruled out the diagnosis before adaptive functioning was ever assessed. Johnson's initial state habeas application, denied 2010, and federal petition, filed June 2011, denied in 2013 to 14, affirmed in 2015, cert denied 2016, raised no Atkins claim. They invoked Atkins only to argue that it should be extended to the mentally ill. In May 2013, while the federal petition was pending, the American Psychiatric Association published the DSM-5, which moved the diagnosis away from IQ cutoffs toward clinical judgment and adaptive functioning. This Court then rejected a rigid IQ cutoff in Hall versus Florida, from 2014, and Texas's Briseno factors in Moore versus Texas, from 2017, and the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals adopted the DSM-5 in 2018. Facing a 2019 execution date, Johnson obtained a full-scale IQ score of 70 and two expert diagnoses of intellectual disability under the DSM-5. Dr. Watson declared that his trial-era scores would not automatically preclude the diagnosis under current standards. The Court of Criminal Appeals dismissed two successive state applications, the first as an abuse of the writ.

2026-11-09_25-159_hoffmann-v-wbi-energy.title: 11/9/26 – Prep: Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc.
2026-11-09_25-159_hoffmann-v-wbi-energy.description: In 2018 WBI invoked section 717f h to condemn easements across the petitioners' ranchland in the Bakken for a roughly 12-mile gas line after the owners, who had been paid more by oil pipelines that lack condemnation power, turned down its offers; once the district court let the owners use evidence of arm's-length easement sales, the parties settled the easements' value in 2021 and reserved the question of fees. The district court applied United States versus Kimbell Foods, found that all three of its factors favored borrowing North Dakota law, under which a court may award a condemnee reasonable fees and costs, N.D. Cent. Code section 32-15-32, and ordered WBI to pay. The Eighth Circuit vacated: under PennEast the statute is a "categorical" delegation of the federal eminent-domain power, so WBI stepped into the United States' shoes; the Fifth Amendment fills any gap, leaving no room for Kimbell Foods; and under Bodcaw, fees are not part of constitutional just compensation unless Congress provides them as "legislative grace." Policy concerns, the panel said, are for Congress.

2026-11-09_25-417_nielsen-v-watanabe.title: 11/9/26 – Prep: Nielsen v. Watanabe
2026-11-09_25-417_nielsen-v-watanabe.description: Watanabe alleges that after he was beaten with a "lock in a sock" in a July 2021 gang riot at the Honolulu detention center, Nielsen heard him rate his back pain a 10, told him to "stop being a cry baby," and refused to send him to a hospital. He says he then got little beyond over-the-counter pain medicine until a February 2022 x-ray showed a fractured coccyx with bone chips in the surrounding tissue. Nielsen points to records showing he gave an anti-inflammatory injection and prescription ibuprofen after consulting an on-call physician. The district court dismissed the $3 million suit as a new context, because the injury was far less severe than Carlson's fatal emergency and because Carlson never considered the Bureau of Prisons' Administrative Remedy Program, ARP. A divided Ninth Circuit panel reversed. Judge Paez, joined by Judge Koh, applied Abbasi's factors, called the claim "identical to Carlson in all meaningful respects," held that a plaintiff "need not suffer death or a life-threatening injury," and treated alternative remedies as a question for step two. It never reached step two; Watanabe had conceded that if the context is new, special factors bar the claim there. Judge Milan Smith dissented on both severity and the ARP.

2026-11-10_25-966_dol-v-sun-valley-orcha.title: 11/10/26 – Prep: Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC
2026-11-10_25-966_dol-v-sun-valley-orcha.description: In 2015 Sun Valley brought in 96 H-2A workers and employed 51 domestic workers alongside them under a job order, which serves as the work contract, promising free housing, kitchen facilities and transportation and the "three-fourths guarantee" of hours. After a Wage and Hour Division investigation and a hearing, an ALJ and D O L's Administrative Review Board found that the farm replaced kitchen access with undisclosed meal charges, profited on drinks deducted from pay, provided substandard housing and vehicles with worn tires and unlicensed drivers, and sent workers home early on forms saying they had left voluntarily. They ordered $211,800 in civil penalties and $344,945.80 in back wages under section 1188 g 2, which authorizes the Secretary "to take such actions, including imposing appropriate penalties and seeking appropriate injunctive relief and specific performance of contractual obligations, as may be necessary to assure employer compliance." The district court dismissed Sun Valley's APA suit on public-rights grounds. The Third Circuit reversed under Jarkesy, holding that D O L had litigated what amounted to a breach-of-contract claim for common-law remedies, penalties, and back wages imposed partly to deter, and that the immigration strand of public rights covers matters close to admitting and excluding aliens, not "rules about worker hours, housing, cooking, and transportation." The panel suggested D O L could still debar the farm through agency proceedings, rejected the government's waiver argument, and did not reach the statutory, Article Two or Eighth Amendment claims. There is no circuit split; the government sought review because, in its view, a federal statute had been invalidated.
